questions.title: Find the differential equation of the family of all circles which touch the $x$-axis at the origin, i.e. $$x^2 + (y-a)^2
questions.html:
basicformation
Find the differential equation of the family of all circles which touch the x-axis at the origin, i.e. x2+(y−a)2=a2⟺x2+y2=2ay, where a is the single arbitrary parameter.

One parameter means differentiate **once**, then eliminate a using the original equation and its derivative together.
Solve for the parameter first: yx2+y2​=2a. Now differentiate that with respect to x — but do not throw away the y′ terms from the denominator.
y2y(2x+2yy′)−(x2+y2)y′​=0⇒2xy+y2y′−x2y′=0, and the y2y′ combines with −x2y′.

There is **one** parameter a, so differentiate once and eliminate it. **Step 1 — isolate the parameter.** x2+y2=2ay⟹yx2+y2​=2a. **Step 2 — differentiate.** y2y(2x+2yy′)−(x2+y2)y′​=0. **Step 3 — clear and simplify the numerator.** 2xy+2y2y′−x2y′−y2y′=0⟹2xy+y2y′−x2y′=0. **Step 4 — group.** (y2−x2)dxdy​+2xy=0​. The parameter a is gone, and the resulting equation is first order — as it must be, since the family had one parameter. *Verification:* with y=a±a2−x2​, so y′=∓a2−x2​x​ and y2−x2=2a(a±⋅​)∓…, direct symbolic substitution reduces (y2−x2)y′+2xy to 0 identically for every a and both branches.

questions.title: Find the differential equation of the family of all non-vertical straight lines $$y = mx + c,$$ where $m$ and $c$ are ar
questions.html:
basicformation
Find the differential equation of the family of all non-vertical straight lines y=mx+c, where m and c are arbitrary constants.

Count the parameters first: m and c are both arbitrary, so how many times must you differentiate?
y′=m kills m; y′′=0 kills c. The straightness of a line is expressed by its vanishing second derivative.
Differentiate twice: y′=m, then y′′=0. That relation has no constants left in it.

The family y=mx+c has **two** essential parameters, m and c, so the differential equation must be of order 2. Differentiate once: y′=m⟹m=y′. Differentiate a second time: y′′=0. Both m and c have disappeared without ever needing to be substituted back — the two differentiations have produced exactly the two equations needed to eliminate them. Hence the differential equation of the family of all straight lines is y′′=0, which has order 2 and degree 1. Geometrically this is exactly "curvature is zero everywhere". (Vertical lines are missed only because they cannot be written as y=f(x); that is why the question says *non-vertical*.)

questions.title: Form the differential equation of the one-parameter family $$y = ce^{2x}.$$ Give the equation in the form $F(x,y,y') = 0
questions.html:
basicformation
Form the differential equation of the one-parameter family y=ce2x. Give the equation in the form F(x,y,y′)=0.

One parameter c means order 1: differentiate exactly once.
dxdy​=2ce2x. Now compare this with the original equation — y=ce2x.
The two right-hand sides differ by a factor 2, so y′=2y, i.e. y′−2y=0.

One parameter c ⟹ differentiate once. y=ce2x⟹dxdy​=2ce2x. Now eliminate c without substituting it explicitly. Since y=ce2x, the derivative equation reads y′=2(ce2x)=2y. So the differential equation of the family is y′−2y=0, first order and first degree — as it must be for a one-parameter family. *Verification:* for y=ce2x, y′−2y=2ce2x−2ce2x=0 identically for every c.

questions.title: Solve $\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{x^2+y^2}{2xy}$.
questions.html:
basichomogeneous
Solve dxdy​=2xyx2+y2​.

Check the degree of the numerator and denominator: both are degree 2 in (x,y). What does that tell you about 2xyx2+y2​?
It is a function of xy​ alone, so put y=vx and use y′=v+xdxdv​. Then isolate xdxdv​.
You get 1−v22v​dv=xdx​, which integrates to x(1−v2)=K. Replace v=xy​ and multiply through.

f(x,y)=2xyx2+y2​ is homogeneous of degree 0 (numerator and denominator both scale like λ2), so it depends only on xy​. Put y=vx, so y′=v+xdxdv​: v+xdxdv​=2x⋅vxx2+v2x2​=2v1+v2​ Isolate the v′-term: xdxdv​=2v1+v2​−v=2v1−v2​ Separate and integrate: 1−v22v​dv=xdx​⟹−ln∣1−v2∣=ln∣x∣+C Exponentiate and absorb constants: x(1−v2)=K. Back-substitute v=xy​: x(1−x2y2​)=xx2−y2​=K x2−y2=Cx​ **Check.** Differentiating x2−y2=Cx: 2x−2yy′=C=xx2−y2​, so y′=2y2x−xx2−y2​​=2xyx2+y2​ ✓

questions.title: Solve $\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{y}{x} + \cos\left(\frac{y}{x}\right)$.
questions.html:
basichomogeneous
Solve dxdy​=xy​+cos(xy​).

Both terms on the right contain y only through xy​. That is exactly the homogeneous pattern, so use the standard substitution.
Put y=vx so y′=v+xdxdv​. The v's will cancel on both sides, leaving xdxdv​=cosv.
cosvdv​=xdx​ integrates with ∫secvdv=ln∣secv+tanv∣, so secv+tanv=C∣x∣. Substitute v=xy​.

The right side is xy​+cosxy​, a function of xy​ only — homogeneous. Put y=vx, so dxdy​=v+xdxdv​: v+xdxdv​=v+cosv The v terms cancel: xdxdv​=cosv Separate: cosvdv​=xdx​ Integrate, using ∫secvdv=ln∣secv+tanv∣: ln∣secv+tanv∣=ln∣x∣+C Exponentiate (and take x>0): secv+tanv=Cx Back-substitute v=xy​: secxy​+tanxy​=Cx​ **Check.** Differentiate secv+tanv=Cx with v=y/x: secv(secv+tanv)(xv​+dxdv​)=C Substituting secv+tanv=Cx and dividing: xsecv(v+xdxdv​)=1⟹v+xdxdv​=cosv which is exactly dxdy​=xy​+cosxy​. Good. (Equivalently tan(4π​+2xy​)=Cx, since secv+tanv=tan(4π​+2v​).)

questions.title: Find the order and degree of the equation $$\left(\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}\right)^3 + y\left(\frac{dy}{dx}\right)^4 = x^5.$$
questions.html:
basicorder-and-degree
Find the order and degree of the equation (dx2d2y​)3+y(dxdy​)4=x5.

Order is simply the highest derivative that appears. Which derivative is highest here?
The equation is already a polynomial in y′ and y′′, so the degree is the power of the highest derivative. Look only at the y′′-term.
Highest derivative is y′′, and it enters as (y′′)3 — a power, not a product of two derivatives.

The derivatives present are y′ and y′′, so the highest one is y′′ and the **order is 2**. The equation is already free of radicals and fractions in the derivatives, and every derivative enters as a whole power — it is a polynomial in y′,y′′. So the **degree is defined**, and it is the power of the highest-order derivative y′′. The y′′-term is (y′′)3, so its power is 3: **degree =3**. (The term y(y′)4 has degree 4 in y′, but the degree is read off the *highest-order* derivative, not the largest power anywhere in the equation. That is why degree is 3 and not 4.)

questions.title: Find the order and degree of $$\left[1+\left(\frac{dy}{dx}\right)^2\right]^{3/2} = k\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}, \quad k \neq 0 .$
questions.html:
basicorder-and-degree
Find the order and degree of [1+(dxdy​)2]3/2=kdx2d2y​,k=0.

The fractional power 3/2 means the equation is not yet a polynomial in the derivatives. You must clear it before the degree can even be read.
Square both sides — that turns [⋯]3/2 into [⋯]3. Then look at the power of y′′.
After squaring: [1+(y′)2]3=k2(y′′)2. Order stays 2; the exponent on y′′ is now 2.

The highest derivative present is y′′, so the **order is 2** and this never changes. For the degree we must first clear the fractional power 3/2. Square both sides: [1+(y′)2]3=k2(y′′)2. This is now a polynomial in y′ and y′′ (the 3 in the bracket is just a power on a whole expression, not a fractional exponent on a derivative). The highest-order derivative y′′ now appears squared, so the **degree is 2**. Note the trap: the 3 on the left bracket is *not* the degree — the degree is the power of the highest-order derivative y′′, which is 2.

questions.title: Find the order and degree of $$\frac{d^2y}{dx^2} + \sin\left(\frac{dy}{dx}\right) = 0.$$
questions.html:
basicorder-and-degree
Find the order and degree of dx2d2y​+sin(dxdy​)=0.

Degree asks a separate question from order: can you write the equation as a polynomial in y′,y′′,…? Ask that of the sin term.
sin(y′)=y′−3!(y′)3​+5!(y′)5​−… — powers of y′ that never stop. Is that a polynomial?
The derivative is *trapped inside* sin and cannot be freed algebraically, so there is no highest power to read off.

**Order.** The highest derivative appearing is y′′, so the order is 2. (Order is always defined.) **Degree.** Expand the sine term: sin(y′)=y′−3!(y′)3​+5!(y′)5​−7!(y′)7​+⋯ The powers of y′ run 1,3,5,7,… without bound, so there is no finite highest power and the expression is not a polynomial in y′. The derivative is trapped inside the transcendental function sin(⋅) and cannot be freed by any algebraic manoeuvre. Therefore the **degree is not defined**. A student who says "degree 1 because the y′′-term is linear" has confused order with degree: linear in y′′ is irrelevant while y′ sits inside a sine.

questions.title: Solve $\frac{dy}{dx} = (1+x)(1+y)$.
questions.html:
basicvariable-separable
Solve dxdy​=(1+x)(1+y).

Factor the right side as f(x)g(y). If you can move every y-part to one side and every x-part to the other, the variables have separated.
You get 1+ydy​=(1+x)dx. Integrate both sides and add C at the moment you integrate — not afterwards.
ln∣1+y∣=x+2x2​+C, so 1+y=Aex+x2/2. Replace ±eC by a single arbitrary constant A and solve for y.

The right side factors: f(x)=1+x, g(y)=1+y. Divide both sides by 1+y: 1+ydy​=(1+x)dx Integrate, adding C at this moment: ln∣1+y∣=∫(1+x)dx=x+2x2​+C Exponentiate and fold the sign into the constant (A=±eC, any non-zero constant): 1+y=Aex+x2/2⟹y=Aex+x2/2−1​ **Check.** dxd​(Aex+x2/2−1)=Aex+x2/2(1+x)=(1+x)(1+y), which is the original right side. Good. **Caveat.** Dividing by 1+y loses the constant solution y=−1; substituting it back confirms it also satisfies the original equation.

questions.title: Solve $\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{1}{x + 2y + 1}$.
questions.html:
basicvariable-separable
Solve dxdy​=x+2y+11​.

The right side mixes x and y inside one linear expression, so you cannot separate yet. Look at the combination x+2y — that is the whole story.
Put u=x+2y+1 and use the chain rule: dxdu​=1+2dxdy​=1+u2​. That equation separates in u and x.
u+2u​du=dx integrates to u−2ln∣u+2∣=x+C. Substitute u=x+2y+1 back, and the lone x on the right cancels the one on the left.

This is the "f(ax+by+c)" pattern. Put u=x+2y+1 Chain rule (do not forget the product rule!): dxdu​=1+2dxdy​=1+u2​=uu+2​ Separate: u+2u​du=dx Integrate. Split u=(u+2)−2: ∫(1−u+22​)du=u−2ln∣u+2∣=x+C Back-substitute u=x+2y+1 (so u+2=x+2y+3): x+2y+1−2ln∣x+2y+3∣=x+C which simplifies to 2y+1−2ln∣x+2y+3∣=C​ **Check.** Differentiating the implicit relation gives 2y′−x+2y+32(1+2y′)​=0⟹y′(x+2y+3)=1+2y′⟹y′(x+2y+1)=1, so y′=x+2y+11​. Exactly the original equation.

questions.title: The population $p$ of a colony satisfies $\frac{dp}{dt} = \frac{1}{2}p - 450$ with $p(0) = 850$. Find the time at which
questions.html:
basicvariable-separable
The population p of a colony satisfies dtdp​=21​p−450 with p(0)=850. Find the time at which the population first becomes zero.

Look at dtdp​=21​p−450: is there any term that mixes p and t? If not, the variables are already separated.
Write the right side as 21​(p−900) so that p sits alone in a difference. That gives p−900dp​=21​dt.
ln∣p−900∣=2t​+C, and p(0)=850 gives C=ln50. So p(t)=900−50et/2. Now set p=0 and solve for t.

Nothing mixes p and t, so separate immediately. Factor the right side: dtdp​=21​(p−900)⟹p−900dp​=21​dt Integrate: ln∣p−900∣=2t​+C Use p(0)=850: ln50=C, so ∣p−900∣=50et/2. Since the population starts below 900 and p′<0, take p−900=−50et/2: p(t)=900−50et/2 **Check.** p′=−25et/2 and 21​p−450=450−25et/2−450=−25et/2. Also p(0)=900−50=850. Good. Population hits zero when 900=50et/2⟹et/2=18⟹t=2ln18​ (equivalently t=ln324≈5.78 time units).

questions.title: Find the differential equation of the family of all parabolas whose axis is parallel to the $x$-axis: $$(y-k)^2 = 4a(x-h
questions.html:
JEE Mainformation
Find the differential equation of the family of all parabolas whose axis is parallel to the x-axis: (y−k)2=4a(x−h), with h,k,a three arbitrary parameters.

Three parameters means differentiate three times. But do **not** try to expand (y−k)2 first — differentiate in the factored form where y−k appears as a single block.
First derivative: (y−k)y′=2a, so y−k=2a/y′. Second: (y′)2+(y−k)y′′=0. Notice a is already gone — you only need y−k.
Substitute y−k=−y′′(y′)2​ into the second derivative relation and clear the y′′: 3y′y′′−y′′(y′)2y′′′​=0.

Three parameters (h,k,a) ⟹ differentiate three times. Keep (y−k) unexpanded so it behaves as one block. **First derivative.** 2(y−k)y′=4a⟹(y−k)y′=2a⟹y−k=y′2a​. **Second derivative.** (y′)2+(y−k)y′′=0⟹y−k=−y′′(y′)2​. **Third derivative** (differentiate the second-derivative equation directly): 2y′y′′+y′y′′+(y−k)y′′′=0. **Substitute** y−k=−y′′(y′)2​: 3y′y′′−y′′(y′)2y′′′​=0. **Clear y′′:** 3(y′′)2−y′y′′′=0​, of order 3 and degree 1 — matching the three parameters h,k,a. *Verification:* writing y=k±2a(x−h)​ and differentiating through to y′′′, the residual 3(y′′)2−y′y′′′ simplifies to exactly 0 for several exact parameter triples, e.g. (a,k,h)=(1,21​,51​) and (2,−1,101​), on both branches.

questions.title: The differential equation of the family of curves $$x^2 = 4b(y + b), \quad b \in \mathbb{R} \text{ arbitrary},$$ is:
questions.html:
JEE MainformationJEE Main 2020
The differential equation of the family of curves x2=4b(y+b),b∈R arbitrary, is:

There is one parameter b, so differentiate once. Key convention: b is a *constant of the family*, so b′=0 when you differentiate.
x2=4by+4b2⇒2x=4by′+0, hence b=2y′x​.
Put b=2y′x​ back into x2=4by+4b2, multiply by (y′)2 and divide by x: you land on x(y′)2=x+2yy′.

There is **one** parameter b, so differentiate once. **Step 1 — differentiate.** This is a family of parabolas with axis along the y-axis. Since b is an arbitrary *constant* of the family, it has derivative 0: 2x=4by′+8b⋅0=4by′⟹b=2y′x​. **Step 2 — substitute back** into x2=4by+4b2: x2=4(2y′x​)y+4(2y′x​)2=y′2xy​+(y′)2x2​. **Step 4 — multiply by (y′)2 and divide by x=0:** x2(y′)2=2xyy′+x2⟹x(y′)2=x+2yy′​. Hence option **(3)**. *Verification:* with y=4bx2​−b we get y′=2bx​, so x(y′)2=4b2x3​ and x+2yy′=x+2(4bx2​−b)2bx​=x+4b2x3​−x=4b2x3​. Identical, for every b.

questions.title: Form the differential equation of the family of confocal, coaxial parabolas $$y^2 = 4a(x+a),$$ where $a$ is the single a
questions.html:
JEE Mainformation
Form the differential equation of the family of confocal, coaxial parabolas y2=4a(x+a), where a is the single arbitrary parameter. (This family is self-orthogonal — check that in your solution.)

One parameter a ⟹ differentiate once, and the derivative equation gives a in terms of x,y,y′ immediately. Do that first.
2yy′=4a⇒a=2yy′​. Put this back into y2=4a(x+a) — note the x+a also contains a, so a appears twice.
y2=4⋅2yy′​(x+2yy′​)=2xyy′+y2(y′)2. Divide by y.

One parameter a ⟹ differentiate once and eliminate a. **Step 1 — differentiate.** 2yy′=4a⟹a=2yy′​. **Step 2 — substitute back** into y2=4a(x+a), replacing *both* occurrences of a: y2=4(2yy′​)[x+2yy′​]=2yy′x+(yy′)2. **Step 3 — divide by y=0:** y(y′)2+2xy′−y=0​, order 1, degree 2. **Self-orthogonality.** Replace y′ by −y′1​=−dydx​: y(y′1​)2−y′2x​−y=0. Multiplying by (y′)2: y−2xy′−y(y′)2=0, which is exactly the *negative* of the original equation. So the family of orthogonal trajectories is the family itself — a **self-orthogonal** family. *Verification:* with y=±4a(x+a)​, symbolic substitution of y′ into y(y′)2+2xy′−y simplifies to exactly 0 for a=1,2,52​ on both branches.

questions.title: Solve $x\frac{dy}{dx} = y + x\tan\left(\frac{y}{x}\right)$ subject to $y(1) = \frac{\pi}{2}$. Express $y$ explicitly.
questions.html:
JEE Mainhomogeneous
Solve xdxdy​=y+xtan(xy​) subject to y(1)=2π​. Express y explicitly.

Divide by x to see the structure: dxdy​=xy​+tanxy​. Both terms are functions of xy​, so it is homogeneous.
Put y=vx: then v+xdxdv​=v+tanv, so xdxdv​=tanv and cotvdv=xdx​. Integrating gives sinv=Cx.
y(1)=2π​ means v(1)=2π​, so C=1. So sinxy​=x — solve that for y (take the branch through y=2π​ at x=1).

Divide by x: dxdy​=xy​+tanxy​ The right side depends on xy​ only, so put y=vx with dxdy​=v+xdxdv​: v+xdxdv​=v+tanv⟹xdxdv​=tanv Separate: tanvdv​=xdx​⟹cotvdv=xdx​ Integrate (with ∫cotvdv=ln∣sinv∣): ln∣sinv∣=ln∣x∣+C⟹sinv=Cx Back-substitute: sinxy​=Cx Use y(1)=2π​: sin1π/2​=1=C⋅1, so C=1 and sinxy​=x. Solving for y (branch through y=2π​): y=xsin−1x​ **Check.** y′=sin−1x+1−x2​x​, while xy​+tanxy​=sin−1x+tan(sin−1x)=sin−1x+1−x2​x​. Identical. Good.

questions.title: A curve passes through $\left(1, \frac{\pi}{6}\right)$. Let the slope of the curve at each point $(x,y)$ be $\frac{y}{x}
questions.html:
JEE MainhomogeneousJEE Advanced 2013
A curve passes through (1,6π​). Let the slope of the curve at each point (x,y) be xy​+sec(xy​), for x>0. Then the equation of the curve is:

The slope is a function of xy​ alone, so this is a homogeneous equation. Use y=vx so that dxdy​=v+xdxdv​.
The v terms cancel again, leaving xdxdv​=secv. Then cosvdv=xdx​, which integrates to sinv=lnx+C.
At (1,6π​) you have v=6π​ and ln1=0, so sin6π​=C=21​.

dxdy​=xy​+secxy​ is a function of xy​ only — homogeneous. Put y=vx: v+xdxdv​=v+secv⟹xdxdv​=secv Separate: secvdv​=xdx​⟹cosvdv=xdx​ Integrate: sinv=lnx+C Back-substitute: sinxy​=lnx+C The curve passes through (1,6π​): sin1π/6​=ln1+C, so 21​=C. sin(xy​)=lnx+21​​ **Check.** Writing y=xarcsin(lnx+21​) and differentiating gives y′=xy​+xcos(y/x)1​=xy​+secxy​. Good.

questions.title: If $y = y(x)$ solves $2x^2\frac{dy}{dx} - 2xy + 3y^2 = 0$ and $y(e) = \frac{e}{3}$, then $y(1)$ is equal to:
questions.html:
JEE MainhomogeneousJEE Main 2022
If y=y(x) solves 2x2dxdy​−2xy+3y2=0 and y(e)=3e​, then y(1) is equal to:

Rewrite it as dxdy​=xy​−23​(xy​)2. Both powers of y come with matching powers of x, so this is homogeneous.
Put y=vx: v+xdxdv​=v−23​v2, hence v2dv​=−23​xdx​ and v1​=23​lnx+C.
Back-substitute v=xy​ to get y2x​=3lnx+C′, then use y(e)=3e​ to find C′. Finally put x=1, where ln1=0.

Rewrite the equation: dxdy​=2x22xy−3y2​=xy​−23​(xy​)2 Every y-power is matched by the same power of x, so the right side is a function of xy​ — homogeneous. Put y=vx: v+xdxdv​=v−23​v2⟹xdxdv​=−23​v2 Separate and integrate: v2dv​=−23​xdx​⟹−v1​=−23​ln∣x∣+C⟹v1​=23​lnx+C Back-substitute v=xy​: yx​=23​lnx+C⟹y2x​=3lnx+C′ So y=3lnx+C′2x​. Use y(e)=3e​: e/32e​=3lne+C′⟹6=3+C′⟹C′=3 y(x)=3(lnx+1)2x​ **Check.** With y=3(lnx+1)2x​ one gets y′=3(lnx+1)22lnx​ and 2x2y′−2xy+3y2=3(lnx+1)24x2[lnx−(lnx+1)+1]​=0. Good. Finally, ln1=0, so y(1)=3(0+1)2​=32​

questions.title: Solve $\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{x+y}{x-y}$.
questions.html:
JEE Mainhomogeneous
Solve dxdy​=x−yx+y​.

Divide top and bottom by x: 1−y/x1+y/x​. The right side is a function of xy​ only, so it is homogeneous.
Put y=vx: v+xdxdv​=1−v1+v​, and the subtler part is 1−v1+v​−v. You will need 1+v21−v​dv=xdx​.
arctanv−21​ln(1+v2)=ln∣x∣+C. Replace ln(1+v2) by ln(x2+y2)−2ln∣x∣ — the ln∣x∣ terms cancel.

x−yx+y​=1−v1+v​ with v=xy​: the right side depends only on v, so the equation is homogeneous. Put y=vx, so y′=v+xdxdv​: v+xdxdv​=1−v1+v​ Isolate the v′-term: xdxdv​=1−v1+v​−v=1−v1+v−v+v2​=1−v1+v2​ Separate: 1+v21−v​dv=xdx​ Integrate both halves: arctanv−21​ln(1+v2)=ln∣x∣+C Back-substitute v=xy​, and use ln(1+x2y2​)=ln(x2+y2)−2ln∣x∣: arctanxy​−21​ln(x2+y2)+ln∣x∣=ln∣x∣+C The ln∣x∣ terms cancel: arctanxy​−21​ln(x2+y2)=C⟹2arctanxy​−ln(x2+y2)=C​ **Check.** Differentiating 2arctanxy​−ln(x2+y2)=C with respect to x gives x2+y22(xy′−y)​−x2+y22x+2yy′​=0⟹xy′−y=x+yy′⟹y′(x−y)=x+y which is exactly y′=x−yx+y​. Good.

questions.title: Solve $\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{2x - y + 1}{x + 3y - 2}$.
questions.html:
JEE Mainhomogeneous
Solve dxdy​=x+3y−22x−y+1​.

This is a linear fractional equation a2​x+b2​y+c2​a1​x+b1​y+c1​​. Read off the coefficients: a1​=2, b1​=−1, a2​=1, b2​=3. What is b1​+a2​?
b1​+a2​=−1+1=0, so the cross coefficients are negatives (Case 3). Cross-multiply and group the differentials: xdy+ydx is d(xy).
Group the remaining pieces as 3ydy=d(23​y2), 2xdx=d(x2), 2dy and dx integrate directly, then add C at the end.

The equation is of the form dxdy​=a2​x+b2​y+c2​a1​x+b1​y+c1​​ with a1​=2, b1​=−1, c1​=1, a2​=1, b2​=3, c2​=−2. Since b1​+a2​=−1+1=0, the cross coefficients are negatives — the equation integrates into exact differentials without any substitution. Cross-multiply: (x+3y−2)dy=(2x−y+1)dx Move everything to one side: 3ydy−2dy+xdy−2xdx−dx+ydx=0 Now recognise the pieces: xdy+ydx=d(xy),3ydy=d(23​y2),2xdx=d(x2) So d(23​y2)+d(xy)−d(x2)−2dy−dx=0 Integrating term by term: 23​y2+xy−x2−2y−x=C​ **Check.** Differentiating gives (3y+x−2)y′+y−2x−1=0, i.e. (x+3y−2)y′=2x−y+1, which is exactly the original equation. Good.

questions.title: Find the order and degree of $$e^{\frac{d^3y}{dx^3} - x\frac{dy}{dx} + y} = 0.$$
questions.html:
JEE Mainorder-and-degree
Find the order and degree of edx3d3y​−xdxdy​+y=0.

As written this does not look like a polynomial in the derivatives — but one cheap algebraic move frees every derivative. Take the natural log of both sides.
eW=0 forces the exponent W to be 0. So dx3d3y​−xdxdy​+y=0.
Now it is a polynomial: highest derivative y′′′ appears to the first power only.

Take the natural logarithm of both sides: dx3d3y​−xdxdy​+y=0. Now every derivative enters algebraically, so the equation is a polynomial in y′,y′′,y′′′ and the degree is defined. - Highest derivative present: y′′′ ⟹ **order =3**. - Power of y′′′: it appears only to the first power ⟹ **degree =1**. This is the standard "escape the exponential" move. The e(⋅)=0 shell hides a perfectly ordinary linear equation; had the derivative been inside a sin instead, the degree would have been undefined.

questions.title: Find the order and degree of $$y = x\frac{dy}{dx} + \frac{k}{dy/dx}.$$
questions.html:
JEE Mainorder-and-degree
Find the order and degree of y=xdxdy​+dy/dxk​.

Only y′ appears anywhere — but the denominator dy/dx has to be cleared before the equation counts as a polynomial. What is the derivative order?
Multiply the whole equation by y′: yy′=x(y′)2+k. Read the power of y′ from the right-hand side.
x(y′)2−yy′+k=0 — the highest derivative is y′ and it appears squared, so degree 2.

**Order.** The only derivative in the equation is y′=dxdy​, so the order is 1. **Degree.** The derivative sits in a denominator, so first clear it. Multiply by y′: yy′=x(y′)2+k⟹x(y′)2−yy′+k=0. This is now a polynomial in y′, with y′ appearing to powers 2 and 1. The highest-order derivative is y′ and its highest power is 2, so the **degree is 2**. This is a Clairaut-type equation (y=xp+k/p with p=y′); its order 1 / degree 2 signature is the standard marker, and its singular solution is the envelope y2=4ax.

questions.title: What is the order of the differential equation whose general solution is $$y = c_1e^{\,x+c_2} + c_3e^{\,x+c_4}?$$
questions.html:
JEE Mainorder-and-degree
What is the order of the differential equation whose general solution is y=c1​ex+c2​+c3​ex+c4​?

Order equals the number of **essential** arbitrary constants — not the number of c-symbols you can count.
Factor out the common ex: y=ex(c1​ec2​+c3​ec4​). How many independent quantities remain inside the bracket?
Write A=c1​ec2​ and B=c3​ec4​. Then y=Aex+Bex, which has just two constants — not four.

The order of the differential equation that governs a family equals the number of **essential (independent)** arbitrary constants in that family. Here four symbols appear, but they do not survive as four parameters. Factor out ex: y=ex(c1​ec2​+c3​ec4​)=Aex+Bex, where A=c1​ec2​,B=c3​ec4​. The four symbols have collapsed to exactly two essential constants, so A and B are the only free parameters. Differentiating twice gives y′=Aex+Bex=y and y′′=y′=y, and eliminating A,B from y=Aex+Bex and y′=Aex+Bex forces y′=y. The equation y′−y=0 has order 1. So the **order is 1** (degree 1), not 4.

questions.title: What is the order of the differential equation whose general solution is $$y = c_1\ln(c_2x)?$$
questions.html:
JEE Mainorder-and-degree
What is the order of the differential equation whose general solution is y=c1​ln(c2​x)?

Two constants are written, but before you count them check whether they are *independent*.
ln(c2​x)=lnc2​+lnx, so y=c1​lnx+c1​lnc2​. One constant survives inside c1​lnc2​.
With A=c1​ and B=c1​lnc2​ the family is y=Alnx+B: two genuinely independent parameters.

Expand the logarithm: y=c1​(lnc2​+lnx)=c1​lnx+c1​lnc2​. Now rename the surviving parameters: A=c1​,B=c1​lnc2​. These are two **independent** constants: c2​=eB/A can be recovered from them (for A=0), and c1​=A. So nothing has been lost — the family really is two-dimensional, just written with two symbols. Two essential constants ⟹ **order =2**. Check by elimination. Differentiate twice: y′=xc1​​,y′′=−x2c1​​=−xy′​, so xy′′+y′=0, an equation of order 2 — matching the parameter count. (The contrast with y=c1​ex+c2​ is the point: there c1​ec2​ merged into a *single* constant and the order dropped to 1, whereas here c1​ and c1​lnc2​ stay independent.)

questions.title: The general solution of $(1+x^2)(1+y)\,dy + (1+y^2)(1+x)\,dx = 0$ is:
questions.html:
JEE Mainvariable-separable
The general solution of (1+x2)(1+y)dy+(1+y2)(1+x)dx=0 is:

Both dx and dy carry a product (1+x2)(1+y2)-type factor. Can you divide the whole equation by one product so that each term contains only one variable?
Divide by (1+x2)(1+y2): you get 1+y21+y​dy+1+x21+x​dx=0. Now each numerator must be split into two pieces over its denominator.
1+u21​+21​1+u22u​ gives arctanu+21​ln(1+u2). Apply that to both x and y.

Divide the whole equation by (1+x2)(1+y2) so that each term holds a single variable: 1+y21+y​dy+1+x21+x​dx=0 Split each fraction over its denominator: [1+y21​+21​1+y22y​]dy+[1+x21​+21​1+x22x​]dx=0 Integrate term by term (each bracket is one arctan plus one 21​ln): arctany+21​ln(1+y2)+arctanx+21​ln(1+x2)=C **Check.** Differentiating: 1+x21+x​+1+y2(1+y)y′​=0⟹y′=−(1+x2)(1+y)(1+y2)(1+x)​ which is precisely the original equation dxdy​=−(1+x2)(1+y)(1+y2)(1+x)​. Good. (One may also combine the two arctangents using arctanx+arctany=arctan1−xyx+y​, but the four-term form above is the safer answer.)

questions.title: The solution of $\frac{dy}{dx} = \sin^2(x + 3y) + 5$ is:
questions.html:
JEE Mainvariable-separable
The solution of dxdy​=sin2(x+3y)+5 is:

The right side depends on x and y only through x+3y. Substitute that whole combination as a single variable.
With u=x+3y you get dxdu​=1+3y′, so dxdu​=3sin2u+16. That is separable — but the integrand has sin2 in it, so divide top and bottom by cos2u and put t=tanu.
191​∫t2+(19​4​)2dt​ gives 419​1​arctan(419​tanu​). Put u=x+3y back.

Let u=x+3y. Then dxdu​=1+3dxdy​, so dxdy​=31​(dxdu​−1). Substitute: 31​(dxdu​−1)=sin2u+5⟹dxdu​=3sin2u+16 Separate: ∫3sin2u+16du​=∫dx=x+C Divide numerator and denominator by cos2u (then multiply the numerator by sec2udu): ∫3tan2u+16(1+tan2u)sec2udu​=∫19tan2u+16sec2udu​ Put t=tanu, dt=sec2udu: 191​∫t2+1916​dt​=191​⋅419​​arctan(419​t​)=419​1​arctan(419​tanu​) So 419​1​arctan(419​tan(x+3y)​)=x+C​ **Check.** dud​[419​1​arctan419​tanu​]=3sin2u+161​, exactly the reciprocal of dxdu​. Good.

questions.title: If $e^y\left(\frac{dy}{dx} - 1\right) = e^x$ and $y(0) = 0$, then $y(1)$ is equal to:
questions.html:
JEE Mainvariable-separableJEE Main 2020
If ey(dxdy​−1)=ex and y(0)=0, then y(1) is equal to:

Rewrite it as dxdy​−1=ex−y. The left side is literally the derivative of y−x, so treat y−x as one variable.
Put u=y−x. Then u′=y′−1=e−u, which separates immediately: eudu=dx.
eu=x+C. With u(0)=y(0)−0=0 you get C=1, so y=x+ln(x+1). Plug in x=1.

Write the equation as dxdy​−1=ex−y The left side is the derivative of u=y−x, so substitute u=y−x: dxdu​=e−u Separate: eudu=dx⟹eu=x+C Initial condition: u(0)=y(0)−0=0, so 1=C. Hence ey−x=x+1⟹y=x+ln(x+1)​ **Check.** y′=1+x+11​, so y′−1=x+11​=e−(y−x)=ex−y. Good. Therefore y(1)=1+ln2

questions.title: Let $y = y(x)$ satisfy $(x^2-4)\,dy - (y^2-3y)\,dx = 0$ for $x > 2$, with $y(4) = \frac{3}{2}$ and slope never zero. The
questions.html:
JEE Mainvariable-separableJEE Main 2024
Let y=y(x) satisfy (x2−4)dy−(y2−3y)dx=0 for x>2, with y(4)=23​ and slope never zero. Then y(10) equals:

Write it as dxdy​=x2−4y(y−3)​. Nothing mixes the variables, so separate — but you will need partial fractions on both sides.
y(y−3)1​=31​(y−31​−y1​) and x2−41​=41​(x−21​+x+21​). Integrate to get 31​ln​yy−3​​=41​ln​x+2x−2​​+C.
Use y(4)=23​ to pin the constant: it gives C=41​ln3. At x=10 the right side becomes 43​ln2, so y3−y​=23/4=81/4.

Rearrange: dxdy​=x2−4y(y−3)​ Separate: y(y−3)dy​=x2−4dx​ Partial fractions on both sides: y(y−3)1​=31​(y−31​−y1​),x2−41​=41​(x−21​+x+21​) Integrate: 31​ln​yy−3​​=41​ln​x+2x−2​​+C Apply y(4)=23​: the left side is 31​ln1=0, while the right side is 41​ln31​+C. Hence C=41​ln3. So 31​ln​yy−3​​=41​ln​x+23(x−2)​​ The solution stays in 0<y<3 (since y′=x2−4y(y−3)​<0 there), so y3−y​>0 and the absolute values drop out. Multiplying the equation by 3 and exponentiating: y3−y​=(x+23(x−2)​)3/4 At x=10: x+23(x−2)​=1224​=2, so y3−y​=23/4=81/4⟹3=y(1+81/4) y(10)=1+81/43​​≈1.119 **Check.** Differentiating 31​lny3−y​−41​lnx+23(x−2)​=0 reproduces y′=x2−4y(y−3)​. Good.

questions.title: The solution of the differential equation $\frac{dy}{dx} = (x-y)^2$, when $y(1) = 1$, is:
questions.html:
JEE Mainvariable-separableJEE Main 2019
The solution of the differential equation dxdy​=(x−y)2, when y(1)=1, is:

The right side is the square of x−y, and the derivative of x−y is 1−y′. That extra 1 is the clue: substitute z=x−y.
z′=1−y′=1−z2, which separates: 1−z2dz​=dx, and ∫1−z2dz​=21​ln​1−z1+z​​.
You get loge​​1−x+y1+x−y​​=2x+C. Then y(1)=1 makes the logarithm 0, so C=−2.

Put z=x−y. Then dxdz​=1−y′=1−(x−y)2=1−z2. Separate and integrate: 1−z2dz​=dx⟹21​ln​1−z1+z​​=x+C Substitute z=x−y and multiply by 2: ln​1−x+y1+x−y​​=2x+C Apply y(1)=1: the log of 1 is 0, so 0=2+C, i.e. C=−2: ln​1−x+y1+x−y​​=2(x−1) Flipping the ratio (and remembering lna=−ln(1/a)): −loge​​1+x−y1−x+y​​=2(x−1)​ **Check.** Differentiating −ln1+x−y1−x+y​=2(x−1) gives back dxdy​=(x−y)2. Good.

questions.title: The differential equation of the family of curves $$c(y+c)^2 = x^3,$$ where $c$ is an arbitrary non-zero constant, can b
questions.html:
JEE Advancedformation
The differential equation of the family of curves c(y+c)2=x3, where c is an arbitrary non-zero constant, can be written in the form 12y(y′)2+ax=bx(y′)3. Find a+b.

One parameter c ⟹ differentiate once: 2c(y+c)y′=3x2. Then **divide the derivative equation by the original** — that kills c and (y+c) at the same time.
c(y+c)22c(y+c)y′​=x33x2​⇒y+c2y′​=x3​⇒y+c=32xy′​.
Now c=y+c−y=32xy′​−y. Substitute **both** of these into the original equation and clear the denominators carefully.

**Step 1 — differentiate once.** 2c(y+c)y′=3x2. **Step 2 — divide the derivative equation by the original equation.** This is the move that removes c almost for free: c(y+c)22c(y+c)y′​=x33x2​⟹y+c2y′​=x3​⟹y+c=32xy′​. **Step 3 — recover c.** c=(y+c)−y=32xy′​−y=32xy′−3y​. **Step 4 — put both back** into c(y+c)2=x3: (32xy′−3y​)(32xy′​)2=x3. **Step 5 — clear denominators.** Multiply by 27 and by x2: (2xy′−3y)4x2(y′)2=27x3⟹(y′)2(2xy′−3y)=27x. **Step 6 — expand and rearrange.** 2x(y′)3−3y(y′)2=27x⟹12y(y′)2+27x=8x(y′)3. Comparing with 12y(y′)2+ax=bx(y′)3 gives a=27 and b=8, so a+b=27+8=35​. **Watch the constant factors.** The easy mistake is to write y+c=3xy′​ (dropping the 2) or to end at 12y(y′)2+9x=8x(y′)3 (forgetting the 4 from (2xy′)2). Both give a plausible-looking but wrong coefficient pair. *Verification:* with y=c​x3/2​−c one gets y′=2c​3x​​, and the residual 12y(y′)2+27x−8x(y′)3 simplifies to exactly 0 for c=1,2,31​ on both branches.

questions.title: Find the differential equation of the family of all circles which pass through the origin and whose centre lies on the l
questions.html:
JEE Advancedformation
Find the differential equation of the family of all circles which pass through the origin and whose centre lies on the line y=x.

Write the general circle through the origin as x2+y2+2gx+2fy=0. Its centre is (−g,−f); impose the condition that this lies on y=x.
(−g)=(−f)⇒g=f. So the family is x2+y2+2g(x+y)=0 — one parameter, differentiate once.
2x+2yy′+2g(1+y′)=0⇒g=−1+y′x+yy′​. Substitute into the original and multiply by (1+y′).

**Step 1 — write the family.** A circle through the origin has no constant term: x2+y2+2gx+2fy=0, with centre (−g,−f). **Step 2 — impose "centre on y=x".** The centre must satisfy −g=−f, i.e. g=f. Writing the single parameter as g: x2+y2+2g(x+y)=0. One parameter ⟹ differentiate once. **Step 3 — differentiate.** 2x+2yy′+2g(1+y′)=0⟹g=−1+y′x+yy′​. **Step 4 — substitute** into the family equation: x2+y2−1+y′2(x+y)(x+yy′)​=0. **Step 5 — clear the denominator.** (x2+y2)(1+y′)−2(x+y)(x+yy′)=0. Expanding: x2+y2+(x2+y2)y′−2x2−2xy−2xyy′−2y2y′=0, (−x2+y2−2xy)+(x2−y2−2xy)y′=0. **Step 6 — rearrange into slope form.** (x2−y2−2xy)dxdy​=x2−y2+2xy​ Order 1, degree 1 — correct for a one-parameter family. *Verification:* the circles are x2+y2+2g(x+y)=0, so y=−g±g2−2gx−x2​. Substituting y and y′ into (x2−y2−2xy)y′−(x2−y2+2xy) simplifies to exactly 0 for g=1,2,−23​ on both branches. *Sanity check on the sign:* compare the easy special case "centre on the x-axis", x2+y2=2cx, which is the same computation with f=0; it reproduces dxdy​=2xyy2−x2​ from the tangent-bisector problem.

questions.title: If the solution curve of $\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{x+y-2}{x-y}$ passes through the points $(2, 1)$ and $(k+1, 2)$ with $k >
questions.html:
JEE AdvancedhomogeneousJEE Main 2022
If the solution curve of dxdy​=x−yx+y−2​ passes through the points (2,1) and (k+1,2) with k>0, then:

As it stands the equation is not homogeneous — the −2 and the −y break it. Find where the lines x+y−2=0 and x−y=0 intersect and move the origin there.
They meet at (1,1). Put x=X+1, y=Y+1: the equation becomes dXdY​=X−YX+Y​, now genuinely homogeneous. Use Y=vX.
You get 1+v21−v​dv=XdX​, i.e. arctanv−21​ln(1+v2)=ln∣X∣+C. The ln∣X∣ cancels, leaving 2arctanXY​−ln(X2+Y2)=C. Then use both given points.

dxdy​=x−yx+y−2​ has constant terms, so it is not homogeneous as written. But the lines x+y−2=0 and x−y=0 meet at (1,1), so shift the origin there: x=X+1,y=Y+1 Then x+y−2=X+Y and x−y=X−Y, so dXdY​=X−YX+Y​ which is homogeneous of degree 0. Put Y=vX, so dXdY​=v+XdXdv​: XdXdv​=1−v1+v​−v=1−v1+v2​ Separate: 1+v21−v​dv=XdX​⟹arctanv−21​ln(1+v2)=ln∣X∣+C Since ln(1+v2)=ln(X2+Y2)−2ln∣X∣, the logarithms cancel: 2arctanXY​−ln(X2+Y2)=C Now use the two points. At (2,1): X=1, Y=0, so 0−ln1=0 and hence C=0. The curve is 2arctanXY​=ln(X2+Y2) At (k+1,2): X=k, Y=1, so 2arctank1​=ln(k2+1) 2tan−1(k1​)=loge​(k2+1)​ **Check.** Differentiating 2arctanXY​−ln(X2+Y2)=0 gives Y′(X−Y)=X+Y, i.e. Y′=X−YX+Y​ — the shifted original equation. Good.

questions.title: The solution of $\frac{dy}{dx} = -\left(\frac{x^2+3y^2}{3x^2+y^2}\right)$ with $y(1) = 0$ is:
questions.html:
JEE AdvancedhomogeneousJEE Main 2023
The solution of dxdy​=−(3x2+y2x2+3y2​) with y(1)=0 is:

−3x2+y2x2+3y2​ depends only on xy​, so the equation is homogeneous. But putting y=vx directly produces 4v2+3v+1, which does not factor over the reals — the quadratic forms are not diagonal in (x,y).
Rotate the axes by 45∘: put u=x+y, v=x−y. Then x2+3y2=u2−uv+v2 and 3x2+y2=u2+uv+v2, and the equation collapses to (u2+v2)du=uvdv.
Set w=uv​: then dudv​=w+ududw​=uvu2+v2​=w1+w2​, so wdw=udu​ and w2=2ln∣u∣+C.

Write the equation as (x2+3y2)dx+(3x2+y2)dy=0 **Rotate the axes by 45∘:** put u=x+y, v=x−y, so x=2u+v​, y=2u−v​, dx=2du+dv​, dy=2du−dv​. Then x2+3y2=u2−uv+v2,3x2+y2=u2+uv+v2 Substitute: (u2−uv+v2)(du+dv)+(u2+uv+v2)(du−dv)=0 2(u2+v2)du−2uvdv=0 Now the equation is homogeneous in u,v. Set w=uv​ (so v=wu, dudv​=w+ududw​): w+ududw​=uvu2+v2​=w1+w2​⟹ududw​=w1​ Separate and integrate: wdw=udu​⟹2w2​=ln∣u∣+C i.e. w2=2ln∣u∣+C. With w=x+yx−y​ and u=x+y: (x+y)2(x−y)2​=2ln∣x+y∣+C Apply y(1)=0: the left side is 1 and ln1=0, so C=1. Multiply through by (x+y)2 and use (x−y)2=(x+y)2−4xy: (x+y)2−4xy=(x+y)2+2(x+y)2ln∣x+y∣ −4xy=2(x+y)2ln∣x+y∣ loge​∣x+y∣+(x+y)22xy​=0​ **Check.** With F=ln∣x+y∣+(x+y)22xy​ one finds Fx​=(x+y)3x2+3y2​,Fy​=(x+y)33x2+y2​ so y′=−Fy​Fx​​=−3x2+y2x2+3y2​, exactly the original equation. And F(1,0)=ln1+0=0. Good.

questions.title: What is the order and degree of the differential equation whose general solution is $$y = (c_1+c_2)\cos(x+c_3) - c_4e^{\
questions.html:
JEE Advancedorder-and-degree
What is the order and degree of the differential equation whose general solution is y=(c1​+c2​)cos(x+c3​)−c4​ex+c5​?

Five c-symbols are written. Merge the ones that combine algebraically or through an exponential before you count.
c1​+c2​ is a *single* parameter, and c4​ec5​ is a single parameter. So which three survive?
With A=c1​+c2​, C=c3​, B=c4​ec5​ the family is y=Acos(x+C)−Bex: three parameters ⟹ order 3, and the eliminant y′′′−y′′+y′−y=0 is linear in y′′′ ⟹ degree 1.

Count **essential** constants, then read the degree off the derivative. **Merging the parameters.** c1​+c2​ is one parameter, not two: call it A. Also c4​ex+c5​=ex(c4​ec5​) and c4​ec5​ is one parameter: call it B. Let C=c3​. Then y=Acos(x+C)−Bex with exactly three essential constants A,B,C — all mutually independent, since c1​ and c2​ can be swapped freely and c5​=ln(B/c4​). **Order.** Three parameters ⟹ **order =3**. **Degree.** Three parameters, so differentiate three times: y′=−Asin(x+C)−Bex, y′′=−Acos(x+C)−Bex, y′′′=Asin(x+C)−Bex. Now eliminate A and B by adding and subtracting these: y′+y′′′=−2Bex,y′′+y=−2Bex⟹y′+y′′′=y′′+y, y′′′−y′′+y′−y=0​. That relation involves no constant and no derivative of order above 3, and A,B,C have all dropped out. It is a polynomial in y′,y′′,y′′′ with y′′′ appearing only to the first power, so the **degree is 1**. Order 3, degree 1 — despite five constants being written down.

questions.title: Find the order and degree of $$\left(\frac{d^3y}{dx^3}\right)^2 + \ln\left(\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}\right) = 0.$$
questions.html:
JEE Advancedorder-and-degree
Find the order and degree of (dx3d3y​)2+ln(dx2d2y​)=0.

Order is easy — find the highest derivative. For the degree you must clear the logarithm, and see whether clearing it also frees y′′′.
ln(y′′)=−(y′′′)2 exponentiates to y′′=e−(y′′′)2. That is *not* a polynomial in y′′′ — the derivative is still trapped in an exponential.
The square on y′′′ looks like it should set the degree, but you must first remove the logarithm, and doing so re-traps y′′′. Hence degree undefined.

**Order.** The highest derivative present is y′′′, so **order =3**. **Degree.** You cannot read a degree straight off the (y′′′)2 term, because the equation is not yet a polynomial in the derivatives. Try to clear the logarithm: isolate it and exponentiate, ln(y′′)=−(y′′′)2⟹y′′=e−(y′′′)2. That is not a polynomial in y′′′ — the highest derivative is now trapped inside an exponential, whose series −(y′′′)2+2!(y′′′)4​−⋯ has unbounded powers of y′′′. And you cannot clear both at once: no algebraic identity frees y′′′ from the exponential while keeping y′′ linear. Since the equation cannot be written as a polynomial in y′,y′′,y′′′, the **degree is not defined**. The moral: "power 2 of the highest derivative" only sets the degree *after* the equation is genuinely polynomial. Here it is not.

questions.title: Find the order and degree of $$\ln\left(\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}\right) = ax + by,$$
questions.html:
JEE Advancedorder-and-degree
Find the order and degree of ln(dx2d2y​)=ax+by,

The logarithm has y′′ inside it, so nothing can be read off until you exponentiate. What does ln(y′′)=ax+by become?
y′′=eax+by. The derivative is now out of the transcendental function and sits alone on the left.
Highest derivative y′′ ⟹ order 2; it appears to the first power ⟹ degree 1. (Note the contrast with sin(y′′), where no exponentiation frees the derivative.)

Exponentiate both sides: dx2d2y​=eax+by. Now the derivative is completely free of the transcendental function and stands alone on the left, while the right-hand side depends only on x and y. The equation is a polynomial in the derivatives. - Highest derivative present: y′′ ⟹ **order =2**. - Power of y′′: 1 ⟹ **degree =1**. This is the key discrimination the chapter is built on. ln(y′′)=ax+by has a *defined* degree because exponentiating frees y′′, whereas y′′+sin(y′)=0 has an *undefined* degree because y′ stays trapped in the sine. Undefined degree means only "cannot be made polynomial" — not "there is a logarithm somewhere".

questions.title: Let $y(x)$ be the solution of $\frac{dy}{dx} = 1 + xe^{y-x}$ with $-\sqrt{2} < x < \sqrt{2}$ and $y(0) = 0$. Then the mi

Let y(x) be the solution of dxdy​=1+xey−x with −2​<x<2​ and y(0)=0. Then the minimum value of y(x) on this interval is:

The constant 1 in 1+xey−x is dxd​(x). So the whole left side is dxd​(y−x) — substitute u=y−x.
You get u′=xeu, so e−udu=xdx and −e−u=2x2​+C. With u(0)=0 this gives y(x)=x−ln(1−2x2​).
Now minimise: y′=0 means 1−2x2​+x=0, i.e. x=1±3​. Only x=1−3​ lies in (−2​,2​). Evaluate y there using 1−2x2​=3​−1.

Since dxd​(x)=1, the natural variable is u=y−x: dxdu​=dxdy​−1=xey−x=xeu Separate: e−udu=xdx⟹−e−u=2x2​+C u(0)=y(0)−0=0 gives C=−1, hence e−u=1−2x2​ and u=−ln(1−2x2​)⟹y(x)=x−ln(1−2x2​)​ **Check.** y′=1+1−x2/2x​, and 1+xey−x=1+xeln(1−x2/2)=1+1−x2/2x​. Good. Now minimise. On (−2​,2​) the denominator 1−2x2​ is positive, so y′=0⟺1+x−2x2​=0⟺x=1±3​ Only x=1−3​≈−0.732 is inside the interval (the other root exceeds 2​). The numerator 1+x−x2/2 is negative for x<1−3​ and positive for x>1−3​, so y decreases then increases — a genuine minimum. At x=1−3​: 1−2x2​=1−2(1−3​)2​=1−(2−3​)=3​−1 so ymin​=(1−3​)−loge​(3​−1)​
